name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Features of epidermal structures and appendages

questiontext.text:
Match the epidermal structures listed in List I with their descriptions in List II:

List I List II
A. Root hairs I. Dumb-bell shaped in grasses and regulate stomatal pore
B. Trichomes II. Unicellular elongations that absorb water and minerals
C. Bulliform cells III. Usually multicellular shoot appendages that prevent water loss
D. Guard cells IV. Large, empty, colourless adaxial epidermal cells in grasses

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the characteristics of root hairs
Root hairs are unicellular elongations of the root epidermal cells (epiblema) that play an essential role in absorbing water and mineral nutrients from the soil solution.

Step 2: Identify the characteristics of trichomes
Trichomes are epidermal appendages present on the shoot system. They are typically multicellular, can be branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, and may be secretory. Their primary function is to prevent excessive water loss caused by transpiration.

Step 3: Identify the characteristics of bulliform cells
Bulliform cells are specialized, large, empty, and colourless adaxial epidermal cells found along the veins in grass leaves. When turgid, they expose the leaf surface, and when flaccid under water stress, they cause the leaf to curl inward to minimize water loss.

Step 4: Identify the characteristics of guard cells
Guard cells are specialized cells that flank and enclose the stomatal pore. In dicotyledonous leaves, they are bean-shaped, whereas in grasses, they are dumb-bell shaped with thin outer walls and thickened inner walls, functioning to regulate stomatal opening and closing.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Root hairs pair with Unicellular elongations that absorb water and minerals; Trichomes pair with Usually multicellular shoot appendages that prevent water loss; Bulliform cells pair with Large, empty, colourless adaxial epidermal cells in grasses; Guard cells pair with Dumb-bell shaped in grasses and regulate stomatal pore.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Types and occurrence of plant vascular bundles

questiontext.text:
Match the vascular bundle arrangements listed in List I with the plant organs in List II where they typically occur:

List I List II
A. Radial vascular bundles I. Monocotyledonous stem
B. Conjoint open vascular bundles II. Dicotyledonous stem
C. Conjoint closed vascular bundles III. Roots of flowering plants
D. Polyarch xylem bundles IV. Monocotyledonous root

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate radial vascular bundles
In radial vascular bundles, xylem and phloem strands lie alternately along different radii within the cylinder. This arrangement is the definitive feature of plant roots.

Step 2: Evaluate conjoint open vascular bundles
Conjoint vascular bundles have xylem and phloem situated along the same radius. When an intrafascicular cambium strip is present between xylem and phloem, the bundle retains the capacity for secondary growth and is called open. This occurs in dicotyledonous stems.

Step 3: Evaluate conjoint closed vascular bundles
In monocotyledonous stems, cambium is absent between xylem and phloem within the conjoint vascular bundles. Consequently, they do not produce secondary tissues and are termed closed.

Step 4: Evaluate polyarch xylem condition
Dicotyledonous roots usually possess two to four xylem patches (diarch to tetrarch), whereas monocotyledonous roots typically have more than six xylem bundles, a condition designated as polyarch.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Radial vascular bundles pair with Roots of flowering plants; Conjoint open vascular bundles pair with Dicotyledonous stem; Conjoint closed vascular bundles pair with Monocotyledonous stem; Polyarch xylem bundles pair with Monocotyledonous root.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Tissues of typical young dicotyledonous stem

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical zones of a young dicotyledonous stem in List I with their descriptions in List II:

List I List II
A. Hypodermis I. Semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma above phloem
B. Starch sheath II. Collenchymatous layers providing mechanical strength to young stem
C. Pericycle III. Radially placed parenchymatous cells between vascular bundles
D. Medullary rays IV. Innermost cortical layer containing abundant starch grains

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the nature of hypodermis in dicot stem
The hypodermis of a young dicotyledonous stem is situated immediately beneath the epidermis and consists of a few layers of collenchymatous cells that provide mechanical flexibility and strength to the young growing stem.

Step 2: Examine the nature of starch sheath
The innermost layer of the cortex in a dicot stem is the endodermis. Its cells are barrel-shaped and conspicuously rich in starch grains; hence, it is termed the starch sheath.

Step 3: Examine the nature of pericycle in dicot stem
The pericycle is situated internal to the endodermis and directly above the phloem, where it appears in the form of semi-lunar patches composed of sclerenchymatous tissue.

Step 4: Examine the nature of medullary rays
Medullary rays consist of a few layers of radially elongated, thin-walled parenchymatous cells situated in the interfascicular regions between adjacent vascular bundles.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Hypodermis pairs with Collenchymatous layers providing mechanical strength to young stem; Starch sheath pairs with Innermost cortical layer containing abundant starch grains; Pericycle pairs with Semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma above phloem; Medullary rays pair with Radially placed parenchymatous cells between vascular bundles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Anatomical components of typical dicotyledonous root

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical structures of a sunflower root in List I with their descriptions in List II:

List I List II
A. Casparian strips I. Parenchymatous cells located between xylem and phloem patches
B. Conjunctive tissue II. Site of origin for lateral roots and vascular cambium
C. Pericycle III. Suberin deposition on radial and tangential walls of endodermis
D. Stele IV. Collective term for all tissues lying on the inner side of endodermis

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Casparian strips and their location
Casparian strips are band-like thickenings of a water-impermeable, waxy material called suberin, deposited on the radial and tangential walls of the barrel-shaped endodermal cells in roots.

Step 2: Identify conjunctive tissue
Conjunctive tissue refers to the parenchymatous cells located in the spaces between the alternating strands of xylem and phloem in primary roots.

Step 3: Identify the role of pericycle in dicot roots
In dicot roots, the pericycle consists of thick-walled parenchymatous layers immediately beneath the endodermis. Its cells retain meristematic potential, giving rise to lateral root primordia and part of the vascular cambium during secondary growth.

Step 4: Identify the composition of stele
The stele represents the central cylinder comprising all tissues located interior to the endodermis, specifically including the pericycle, vascular bundles, conjunctive tissue, and pith.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Casparian strips pair with Suberin deposition on radial and tangential walls of endodermis; Conjunctive tissue pairs with Parenchymatous cells located between xylem and phloem patches; Pericycle pairs with Site of origin for lateral roots and vascular cambium; Stele pairs with Collective term for all tissues lying on the inner side of endodermis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Internal structural tissues of angiosperm leaves

questiontext.text:
Match the leaf tissues and structures in List I with their structural features in List II:

List I List II
A. Palisade parenchyma I. Loosely arranged oval or rounded cells with large air cavities
B. Spongy parenchyma II. Vertically elongated cells arranged parallel to each other below adaxial epidermis
C. Bulliform cells III. Layer of thick-walled cells encircling the vascular bundles
D. Bundle sheath cells IV. Large, empty, colourless adaxial cells that roll leaves inward when flaccid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characterize palisade parenchyma
Palisade parenchyma is situated adaxially (towards the upper epidermis) in dorsiventral leaves. It is composed of elongated, columnar parenchymatous cells arranged vertically and parallel to one another, containing numerous chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

Step 2: Characterize spongy parenchyma
Spongy parenchyma is situated beneath the palisade layer and extends to the abaxial (lower) epidermis. It is composed of oval or rounded cells that are loosely arranged, creating conspicuous intercellular spaces and large air cavities for gaseous exchange.

Step 3: Characterize bulliform cells
In grasses, specific adaxial epidermal cells along veins become modified into large, empty, and colourless bulliform cells. During water deficit, these cells lose turgidity and become flaccid, causing the leaves to curl inward to limit transpirational water loss.

Step 4: Characterize bundle sheath cells
Vascular bundles within leaf veins are surrounded by a compact border of parenchymatous or thick-walled cells referred to as bundle sheath cells, isolating the vascular tissues from the mesophyll intercellular spaces.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Palisade parenchyma pairs with Vertically elongated cells arranged parallel to each other below adaxial epidermis; Spongy parenchyma pairs with Loosely arranged oval or rounded cells with large air cavities; Bulliform cells pair with Large, empty, colourless adaxial cells that roll leaves inward when flaccid; Bundle sheath cells pair with Layer of thick-walled cells encircling the vascular bundles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Distinguishing anatomical features of stems and roots

questiontext.text:
Match the plant organs in List I with their primary distinguishing anatomical features in List II:

List I List II
A. Dicot stem I. Scattered closed vascular bundles, absence of phloem parenchyma, and presence of water cavities
B. Monocot stem II. Ring arrangement of conjoint, open vascular bundles with endarch protoxylem
C. Dicot root III. Polyarch xylem bundles with more than six patches and a prominent, large pith
D. Monocot root IV. Diarch to tetrarch xylem bundles with inconspicuous pith and presence of cambium ring later

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify key anatomical markers of dicot stem
A dicotyledonous stem is distinguished by a ring arrangement of vascular bundles, each bundle being conjoint, open (with intrafascicular cambium), and possessing endarch protoxylem where protoxylem points towards the pith.

Step 2: Identify key anatomical markers of monocot stem
A monocotyledonous stem has numerous conjoint closed vascular bundles scattered throughout parenchymatous ground tissue, lacks phloem parenchyma, and contains water-holding cavities within the bundles.

Step 3: Identify key anatomical markers of dicot root
A dicotyledonous root displays 2 to 4 (diarch to tetrarch) alternating xylem and phloem patches, an inconspicuous or tiny pith, and secondary meristem formation later between xylem and phloem.

Step 4: Identify key anatomical markers of monocot root
A monocotyledonous root exhibits a polyarch condition with typically more than six xylem strands and possesses a large, well-developed central parenchymatous pith, lacking secondary growth.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Dicot stem pairs with Ring arrangement of conjoint, open vascular bundles with endarch protoxylem; Monocot stem pairs with Scattered closed vascular bundles, absence of phloem parenchyma, and presence of water cavities; Dicot root pairs with Diarch to tetrarch xylem bundles with inconspicuous pith and presence of cambium ring later; Monocot root pairs with Polyarch xylem bundles with more than six patches and a prominent, large pith.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Classification and constituents of plant tissue systems

questiontext.text:
Match the plant tissue systems and complexes in List I with their constituents in List II:

List I List II
A. Epidermal tissue system I. Complex conducting tissues comprising xylem and phloem
B. Ground tissue system II. Cortex, pericycle, medullary rays, pith, and mesophyll
C. Vascular tissue system III. Stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells
D. Stomatal apparatus IV. Epidermal cells, cuticle, stomata, trichomes, and root hairs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the epidermal tissue system
The epidermal tissue system constitutes the outer boundary covering the entire plant body. It comprises compactly arranged parenchymatous epidermal cells, cuticle (except in roots), stomata, and external appendages such as unicellular root hairs and shoot trichomes.

Step 2: Understand the ground tissue system
The ground or fundamental tissue system encompasses all internal tissues excluding epidermal layers and vascular bundles. It consists of simple tissues (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) making up the cortex, endodermis, pericycle, medullary rays, pith, and leaf mesophyll.

Step 3: Understand the vascular tissue system
The vascular or conducting tissue system is formed by the complex vascular tissues, xylem and phloem, organized into bundles to transport water, dissolved minerals, and organic solutes throughout the plant.

Step 4: Understand the stomatal apparatus
The stomatal apparatus is an integrated functional complex comprising three elements: the central stomatal pore (aperture), the pair of flanking guard cells, and the specialised adjacent epidermal subsidiary cells.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Epidermal tissue system pairs with Epidermal cells, cuticle, stomata, trichomes, and root hairs; Ground tissue system pairs with Cortex, pericycle, medullary rays, pith, and mesophyll; Vascular tissue system pairs with Complex conducting tissues comprising xylem and phloem; Stomatal apparatus pairs with Stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Tissue specializations in dicot and monocot stems

questiontext.text:
Match the tissue specializations in List I with their precise anatomical context in List II:

List I List II
A. Sclerenchymatous bundle sheath I. Innermost layer of cortex in young dicot stem
B. Collenchymatous hypodermis II. Structural cavity formed inside vascular bundles of monocot stem
C. Starch sheath III. Mechanical sub-zone beneath epidermis in young dicot stem
D. Water-containing cavities IV. Sclerenchyma jacket surrounding scattered vascular bundles in monocot stem

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze sclerenchymatous bundle sheath
In monocotyledonous stems, each scattered vascular bundle is individually surrounded by a protective sheath of sclerenchymatous fibres termed the bundle sheath, providing structural rigidity.

Step 2: Analyze collenchymatous hypodermis
In dicotyledonous stems, the hypodermis lies right beneath the epidermis and consists of several layers of collenchyma cells with characteristic pectin-rich corner thickenings that afford tensile mechanical strength.

Step 3: Analyze starch sheath
The endodermis of the young dicot stem forms the innermost boundary of the cortex. Because its barrel-shaped cells store dense starch grains, it is specifically referred to as the starch sheath.

Step 4: Analyze water-containing cavities
In monocot stem vascular bundles, the breakdown and dissolution of earliest protoxylem elements result in distinct protoxylem lacunae, which serve as water-containing cavities.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Sclerenchymatous bundle sheath pairs with Sclerenchyma jacket surrounding scattered vascular bundles in monocot stem; Collenchymatous hypodermis pairs with Mechanical sub-zone beneath epidermis in young dicot stem; Starch sheath pairs with Innermost layer of cortex in young dicot stem; Water-containing cavities pair with Structural cavity formed inside vascular bundles of monocot stem.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Functional roles of specialised plant anatomical tissues

questiontext.text:
Match the specialised plant tissues and cell layers in List I with their functional or developmental significance in List II:

List I List II
A. Pericycle of dicot root I. Meristematic strip producing secondary xylem and phloem
B. Intrafascicular cambium II. Specialised epidermal cells assisting guard cells in stomatal dynamics
C. Subsidiary cells III. Thick-walled parenchyma giving rise to lateral root primordia and vascular cambium
D. Abaxial leaf epidermis IV. Epidermal surface generally possessing a greater density of stomata in dorsiventral leaves

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate pericycle of dicot root
In dicot roots, the pericycle consists of thick-walled parenchymatous cells. During development, these cells undergo dedifferentiation to initiate lateral root branch primordia as well as contributing to the formation of secondary vascular cambium.

Step 2: Evaluate intrafascicular cambium
Intrafascicular cambium is the primary meristematic layer situated between primary xylem and primary phloem in open vascular bundles of dicot stems. By dividing periclinally, it produces secondary xylem internally and secondary phloem externally.

Step 3: Evaluate subsidiary cells
Subsidiary cells are epidermal cells adjacent to the guard cells that become modified in their size, shape, and cytoplasmic content. They play an auxiliary role in stomatal movement by facilitating rapid water exchange with guard cells.

Step 4: Evaluate abaxial epidermis of dorsiventral leaf
In a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf, stomata are distributed unevenly; the lower (abaxial) epidermis typically bears significantly more stomata than the upper (adaxial) epidermis, an adaptation that reduces direct solar evaporation.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Pericycle of dicot root pairs with Thick-walled parenchyma giving rise to lateral root primordia and vascular cambium; Intrafascicular cambium pairs with Meristematic strip producing secondary xylem and phloem; Subsidiary cells pair with Specialised epidermal cells assisting guard cells in stomatal dynamics; Abaxial leaf epidermis pairs with Epidermal surface generally possessing a greater density of stomata in dorsiventral leaves.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Diagnostic anatomical criteria of vegetative plant organs

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical character combinations in List I with the corresponding plant organs in List II:

List I List II
A. Radial vascular bundles, suberised Casparian strips, and 2 to 4 xylem patches I. Monocotyledonous stem
B. Conjoint open vascular bundles in a ring, collenchymatous hypodermis, and starch sheath II. Dicotyledonous root
C. Conjoint closed scattered bundles, sclerenchymatous hypodermis, and absent phloem parenchyma III. Dorsiventral leaf
D. Conjoint bundles in veins, adaxial palisade and abaxial spongy mesophyll IV. Dicotyledonous stem

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagnose the anatomical features of dicotyledonous root
An internal organization with radial bundles arranged on alternating radii, Casparian strips impregnated with suberin in the endodermis, and 2 to 4 (diarch to tetrarch) xylem strands unambiguously diagnoses a primary dicotyledonous root.

Step 2: Diagnose the anatomical features of dicotyledonous stem
The presence of a collenchymatous hypodermis, endodermis rich in starch (starch sheath), and a ring of conjoint, open vascular bundles with endarch protoxylem defines a dicotyledonous stem.

Step 3: Diagnose the anatomical features of monocotyledonous stem
The combination of a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered conjoint closed vascular bundles encircled by sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths, and complete absence of phloem parenchyma characterizes a monocotyledonous stem.

Step 4: Diagnose the anatomical features of dorsiventral leaf
A transverse laminar profile showing conjoint vascular bundles embedded in veins, accompanied by mesophyll differentiated into an upper palisade layer and a lower loosely packed spongy layer, defines a dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs
The correct associations are: Radial vascular bundles, suberised Casparian strips, and 2 to 4 xylem patches pair with Dicotyledonous root; Conjoint open vascular bundles in a ring, collenchymatous hypodermis, and starch sheath pair with Dicotyledonous stem; Conjoint closed scattered bundles, sclerenchymatous hypodermis, and absent phloem parenchyma pair with Monocotyledonous stem; Conjoint bundles in veins, adaxial palisade and abaxial spongy mesophyll pair with Dorsiventral leaf.
